summary: This experimental RFC describes QNAME minimisation, a DNS privacy technique where a resolver sends upstream servers only as much of the query name as they need. This limits what each server learns. It was replaced by RFC 9156.

plainLanguage.summary: Asking for a book at the library, you don't tell every person in the building the title. You only say the part each one needs.

subtitle: A DNS privacy technique that limits information leakage to authoritative servers.

tldr.problem: When a DNS resolver looks up a domain name, it traditionally sends the full domain name (QNAME) to every authoritative server it queries, revealing to each server exactly what the user is looking for.
tldr.mechanism: QNAME minimisation sends only the minimum information necessary: when asking about subdomain zone cuts, the resolver sends queries with shorter names, asking only for the next label boundary rather than the complete original name.
tldr.outcome: Each DNS server in the path learns less about what the user is resolving, improving privacy without changing the DNS protocol. It was later standardized in RFC 9156.

facts.label: QNAME form
facts.value: One label more than zone authority

today: RFC 7816 is Experimental and was obsoleted by RFC 9156, which standardized QNAME minimisation and included refinements based on deployment experience. Most modern DNS resolvers now implement minimisation to improve user privacy.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 7816 describes a DNS privacy technique called QNAME minimisation that reduces the amount of information leakage during DNS name resolution. The problem it addresses is fundamental: in a traditional DNS lookup, when a resolver queries authoritative name servers, it sends the entire domain name being looked up, revealing to each server exactly what domain the user is trying to reach.

The specification applies the principle of data minimization from RFC 6973: the less data you send, the fewer privacy problems you have. Importantly, sending the full QNAME to authoritative servers is a tradition, not a protocol requirement. The DNS RFCs do not mandate it. QNAME minimisation works by a unilateral change in resolver behavior—it does not require changes to the DNS protocol or to authoritative servers.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS is the system that translates domain names (like example.com) to IP addresses. When you look up a name, your computer asks multiple servers along the way. Normally, it tells each server the complete name you're looking for. QNAME minimisation tells each server only the part they actually need.

sections.title: How QNAME Minimisation Works
sections.content:
The resolver that implements QNAME minimisation operates differently from a traditional resolver. Instead of sending the full original QNAME to the upstream name server, it sends a query with the QTYPE set to NS (asking for nameserver records) and the QNAME stripped to just one label more than the zone for which the server is authoritative.

For example, if a resolver knows that ns1.nic.example is authoritative for .example and receives a request to resolve foo.bar.baz.example, it will query ns1.nic.example for NS records for just baz.example—not the full name. The resolver then learns the zone cut for baz.example and continues with deeper queries. Zone cuts (the points where authority delegates from one server to another) do not necessarily align with label boundaries, so the resolver may need to iterate, adding one label at a time until it reaches a zone cut.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine delegations are like asking directions. A traditional resolver asks every person the full destination. A minimising resolver asks: where is the next person I need to ask? Then asks them the next part of the question.

sections.title: Compatibility and Practical Issues
sections.content:
QNAME minimisation is compatible with existing DNS infrastructure because it is a unilateral change to resolver behavior. However, some broken name servers may have problems with it. Some authoritative servers reject NS queries inappropriately, returning REFUSED instead of a proper response. Others incorrectly return NXDOMAIN for Empty Non-Terminals (ENTs), situations where a parent node exists but has no records. These are protocol violations, but they exist in the wild.

A workaround is to fall back to querying with QTYPE=A instead of NS when NS queries fail, since A queries are more widely supported. Another approach is to retry with the full query when receiving an NXDOMAIN response, though this reduces privacy benefits. The RFC recommends implementing minimisation despite these edge cases, as the benefits outweigh the complications.
sections.plainLanguage: Some older DNS servers don't follow the rules properly and get confused by these shorter queries. The spec suggests workarounds like trying a different query type, but overall it's safe to use.

sections.title: Performance Impact
sections.content:
While the primary goal of QNAME minimisation is privacy, it has nuanced performance implications. In some cases it improves performance: if a resolver receives multiple queries for A.example, B.example, and C.example (where .example doesn't exist), a minimising resolver learns once that .example is non-existent and can cache that answer, avoiding three separate NXDOMAINs. It also optimizes lookups for TLDs by reducing queries to two-label QNAMEs.

In other cases it may temporarily degrade performance: for very deep domain names like www.host.group.department.example.com where everything is under example.com's servers, a minimising resolver with an empty cache would send one query per label, whereas traditional iteration would learn the full delegation immediately. However, once the cache warms up, there is no performance difference. The RFC notes that practical testing shows the performance impact is generally minimal.
sections.plainLanguage: Using shorter queries sometimes makes lookups faster (by learning negative answers quicker) and sometimes slower (if you have to ask about each label separately). Overall, the effects mostly cancel out once the system learns the zone structure.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
QNAME minimisation provides privacy benefits by limiting exposure to authoritative name servers. Each server in the resolution chain learns less about what the user is trying to look up. However, the technique offers zero protection against a recursive resolver (a resolver that queries on behalf of the client), which still receives the full query from the client's stub resolver.

For wire sniffers, QNAME minimisation provides partial protection. If an attacker captures network traffic between a resolver and an authoritative server, they will see shorter QNAMEs. However, encryption (such as DNS over HTTPS or DNS over TLS) provides stronger protection against eavesdropping than minimisation alone. DNSSEC-validating resolvers already know zone cuts, so they can implement minimisation easily.
sections.plainLanguage: This protects you from authoritative DNS servers learning what you're looking up. It does not protect you from your own ISP's DNS server (which sees everything). Encryption is better for that.
